6.0.s.en: 1. The prophet's vision in the temple:

6.0.0.en: 1 In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. 2 Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. 3 And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory. 4 And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke.

6.0.1.en: “In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple” [1].

6.0.2.en: The prophet enjoyed this vision in the year of the death of King Uzziah, perhaps after he had announced his earlier prophecies, which carried a threat to the people, and the people met them with aversion and contempt; therefore this vision was revealed to him that he might proclaim it to the people, affirming that he bears a divine message and presents the word of God. Perhaps this vision took place before the prophecies, and the prophet announced it afterward to assure the people that what he utters is not from himself, as St. Paul did when he wished to confirm his apostleship by speaking of the vision that he saw at the beginning of his ministry (2 Cor 12).

6.0.3.en: The vision appeared in the year of the death of King Uzziah, who reigned over Judah at the age of 16 for 52 years and did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, and he prospered in all his works: in wars, in building and rebuilding cities, and so on... But when his name was greatly lifted up he fell into pride and wanted to burn incense to the Lord on the altar of incense, so the Lord struck him with leprosy while he was in the temple, and the priests thrust him out, and he was a leper until the day of his death, isolated in a house far from the king's palace.

6.0.4.en: Perhaps Isaiah had been following with joy the success of Uzziah along with the uprightness of his heart and his growth in the Spirit, but he was very grieved at his fall in his last days, and his dying thus isolated from the people of God, expelled from His holy temple, representing the vanity of temporal glory.

6.0.5.en: The prophet looked at the people in the year of Uzziah's death and saw them cast down like sheep without a shepherd, especially since the king had withdrawn from the people for a time before his death because of his leprosy. Isaiah realized that the people needed heavenly care, because the arm of man is unable to satisfy the needs of the people, and as the psalmist says: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation; their spirit goeth forth, they return to their dust” (Ps 146:3).

6.0.6.en: In the midst of this bitterness the Lord declared this vision to Isaiah for his comfort: the vision most likely took place in the temple at a time when the prophet was alone for private worship, crying out to God to take over the care of His people. The Lord appeared to him sitting on a throne high and lifted up to assure him that He is the heavenly Shepherd of His people, whose thoughts are higher than the thoughts of men and His ways than their ways. He sits on high in order to carry His Church with Him, sharing His heavenly glories. He saw His train filling the temple, for He dwelt in His Church, awaiting every soul that comes to Him to enjoy union with Him. He saw the Lord Christ in His glory (Jn 12:41), filling heaven and earth with His divinity and His care.

6.0.7.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that Isaiah and the other prophets did not see the essence of the divinity as it is, but God appeared to them through His condescension, as much as they could bear the vision, because of His love for His creation; even for the heavenly ones and the bearers of His throne, each of them sees Him according to his capacity, but the essence in itself, that is, in its absolute perfection, cannot be comprehended.

6.0.8.en: * The Seraphim cry out, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth... The heavenly powers are seized by awe without ceasing, so they turn their faces and spread their wings like a wall, to shield them from the unbearable radiance that comes from God, and yet what they see is only a reduced image of the reality...

6.0.9.en: While the Seraphim are not even strong enough to behold God, who is revealed to them only as a condescension on His part according to their weakness, we see people who dare to picture in their minds the very nature that the Seraphim are unable to comprehend. They claim that they are able to look upon it clearly and without limit!

6.0.10.en: Tremble, O heavens, and be astonished, O earth.

6.0.11.en: * Truly God, even for these orders, is incomprehensible and cannot be approached. For this reason He condescends to appear in the way recorded in the vision. God, whom no place contains and who does not sit on a throne... out of His love for us appears seated on a throne, surrounded by the heavenly powers.

6.0.12.en: * These (visions of the prophets) are revelations, all of them examples of His condescension, and not visions of His essence by its disclosure. For if they had beheld His very essence they would not have seen Him under different forms, since He is simple, without form or members or defined manners; His nature does not sit or stand or walk...

6.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom “Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory” [2-3].

6.1.1.en: Perhaps what comforts the soul of the servant is that his heart is lifted up to see the angelic service, and he realizes that all the troubles and weaknesses of the Church will one day end, so that she may share with the heavenly ones in praise forever. And that the Church here, as the icon of heaven, enjoys the pledge of the heavenly service. In one Coptic homily the Church is defined as: [a place of comfort; she is the assembly of the angels and the place of the Cherubim and the Seraphim]. It is said that St. Pachomius the Egyptian used to see the Church filled with angels.

6.1.2.en: The Seraphim are the servants of the divine throne; they bear the Lord with joy and exultation, and praise Him without ceasing. It is as though the work of every servant or prophet in the Church is to draw every soul to the Lord as a throne for Him to dwell in, and to establish His Kingdom within it, so that it becomes like the fiery heavenly Seraph. Each Seraph has 6 wings: with two he covers his face, a sign of his being marked by the fear of God, since he cannot comprehend all the divine splendor; with two he covers his feet, a sign of modesty, if this expression is right; and with two he flies, soaring in the heavenly places. Thus it befits us to be like the Seraph, enjoying the fear of God in modesty with constant growth and continual ascent toward the heavenly places.

6.1.3.en: As for the seraphic hymn, “the Thrice-Holy,” it appears in the writings of Origen; and perhaps the date of its use in Alexandria goes back to an earlier time. It is said in Church tradition that Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who took care of the body of the Lord after it was taken down from the Cross, heard this hymn as they were putting the spices on the body of the Lord before His burial.

6.2.0.en: The Seraphim say: “The whole earth is full of his glory” [3]; not only does it fill the heavens but the whole earth. He dwelt on the earth to raise up heaven from the earth. And as St. Clement of Alexandria says, the earth becomes heaven for the true believer. Although our body in its origin is dust, the Word of God received our human nature to sanctify it, so our body became glorified in Him, and we no longer despise it, because it shares with the soul its worship of God, its striving and its crown.

6.2.1.en: The following is noted in this hymn:

6.2.2.en: A. The word “Lord” came in the plural, Adonai, and not the singular, Adon. Perhaps for this reason, together with the repetition of the word “holy” three times, St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, saw it as proclaiming the glory of the Trinity, while the Apostle Paul attributes it to the Holy Spirit (Acts 28:25-26), and St. John to the Son (Jn 12:41), while ancient Jewish tradition attributes it to the Father.

6.2.3.en: * By means of (the Seraphim) the mystery of the Trinity was clearly proclaimed, when they uttered that wonderful cry “Holy,” as it carries beauty together with awe for each Hypostasis of the Trinity.

6.2.4.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa B. God is called “LORD of hosts,” which is the title of God in His battle against evil or against the powers of darkness, and it has a teaching meaning. It does not appear in the books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, Job, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, but appears rarely in Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and the Psalms; it is used abundantly in the books of the prophets: in Jeremiah it is used about 80 times, in Haggai 14 times, in Zechariah 50 times, and in Malachi more than 24 times. The first to use it was Hannah, the mother of Samuel, in the song of victory which she uttered when she felt that God was the secret of her victory in her inner battle.

6.2.5.en: C. This hymn is used in the Divine Liturgy as a sign of the believers' fellowship with the heavenly ones in worship on a heavenly level, in a spirit of unity and harmony together:

6.2.6.en: * May we gather together in our consciences in agreement and cry to Him earnestly as with one mouth, that we may share in His great and glorious promises.

6.2.7.en: St. Clement of Rome * That you may realize with what awe and fear they utter that name as they glorify Him and praise Him; but you call upon Him in your prayers and petitions with great laxity, although you ought to be filled with awe and be in vigilance with reverence.

6.2.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * The new things go in harmony with the old, and the old with the new. Behold the Seraphim say to one another: Holy, holy, holy, LORD of hosts. The two Testaments go in one melody, and have one voice...

6.3.0.en: St. Augustine “And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke” [4].

6.3.1.en: The foundations of the house of the Lord shook before the cries of the Seraphim glorifying the Holy God, and the house was filled with thick cloud, a sign of the dwelling of the glory of God in it. And when the Lord Christ entered Jerusalem, the city was also moved (Mt 21:10). We need the Lord to declare His dwelling in us, to establish His Kingdom within us, that we may share with the Seraphim their eternal hymn, so that the depths of our souls are shaken with Isaiah the prophet, and the glory of the Lord is declared in us, and our depths are sanctified, so that we are counted witnesses of truth for His Gospel.

6.4.0.en: 5 Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts. 6 Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar: 7 And he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged.

6.4.1.en: When we stand in the presence of the Holy God, His glory is declared to us and we discover our uncleanness, as happened with Isaiah the prophet: “Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts” [5].

6.4.2.en: The Apostle Paul confesses that he is the first of sinners (1 Tim 1:15), not because he thinks about his sins and tries to count them, but as the fruit of his enlightenment by the Spirit of the Holy God, who exposes our depths, so that we discover that we are nothing before the glory of God, and that we are utterly sinners before His holiness. Therefore when Abraham, the father of the fathers, began to speak with God, he said: “Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes” (Gen 17:27).

6.4.3.en: Perhaps Isaiah wanted to share with the Seraphim in their praises to God, and so he realized that he was of unclean lips, and as he looked at the company of the Seraphim in their exultations, he realized that he dwelt among a people of unclean lips.

6.4.4.en: * With daily sighs the saints grieve over the weakness of their nature, and while they search into the change of their thoughts, their will and the depths of their inner consciences, they cry out in supplication, saying: “Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified”... And so they realize the weakness of man's righteousness and its imperfection, together with the constant need of God's mercies. Therefore he whose evils and sins God removed with the coal of “His living word” on the altar, after his wonderful vision of God and of the heavenly Seraphim and his enjoyment of the revelation of the divine mysteries, says: “Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips.”

6.4.5.en: Father Theonas * Behold, you see how all the saints truly confess, not on behalf of the people but rather about themselves, that they are sinners, yet they never despair of their salvation, but look to complete justification by the grace and mercy of the Lord.

6.5.0.en: Father Theonas His sense of the uncleanness of his lips and the uncleanness of the lips of his people did not crush his spirit, but filled him with hope in God, whom he had enjoyed seeing in the vision as the “LORD of hosts,” able to raise up from humanity spiritual soldiers for Himself. This was fulfilled for him, as he said: “Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar: and he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged” [6-7].

6.5.1.en: It is said in the Fraction of the Liturgy of St. Cyril: [As You purified the lips of Your servant Isaiah the prophet when one of the Seraphim took a coal with the tongs from the altar and laid it in his mouth, and said to him: Lo, this hath touched thy lips, it taketh away thine iniquities and purgeth thee from all thy sins; so also we, the weak sinners, Your servants who seek Your mercy, graciously purify our souls, our bodies and our hearts, and give us this true coal, which gives life to the soul, the body and the spirit, which is the holy Body and the precious Blood of Your Christ.]

6.5.2.en: And in another prayer of the Fraction the priest says: [For I have come forward to touch Your Body and Blood out of my longing in Your love; so do not burn me with them, O You who formed me, but burn up all the thorns that choke my soul.]

6.5.3.en: St. Mary bore the Word of God incarnate in her, the burning coal, who sanctifies humanity with His precious blood.

6.6.s.en: 3. The mission of Isaiah the prophet:

6.6.0.en: 8 Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me. 9 And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. 10 Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed. 11 Then said I, Lord, how long? And he answered, Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate, 12 And the LORD have removed men far away, and there be a great forsaking in the midst of the land. 13 And if a tenth remain in it, it shall return and become a waste; but as the terebinth and the oak, which, when they are cut down, have a stock, so its stock shall be a holy seed.

6.6.1.en: When Isaiah the prophet saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and His train filling the temple, and the Seraphim praising Him, and his lips had been cleansed by the divine coal, he longed for the heavenly life and the angelic praise, but at the same time he longed to see his people enjoying this heavenly life, as though he were saying with the Apostle Paul: “Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you” (Phil 1:24). This is also what the prophet declares by saying: “Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me” [8].

6.6.2.en: This is the fifth scene of the same vision, in which he was called to the prophetic work, on behalf of the Kingdom of the Lord; these scenes are: 1. The scene of the Lord in His glory [1]. 2. The scene of the Seraphim praising Him [3]. 3. The shaking of the posts of the door and the filling of the house with smoke [4]. 4. The sanctification of the prophet's lips [5-7]. 5. The call of Isaiah by the voice of God Himself [8 ff.].

6.6.3.en: The call came from God Almighty Himself, and since Isaiah believed in God's saving power and His sanctifying work, he came forward for the work, realizing that where he is weak he is strong in the Lord. When we realize that we are nothing, let us believe in God, all in all, who is able by His Holy Spirit to work through us.

6.6.4.en: Here we must point out that while the speaker is one: “Whom shall I send?” we find Him using the plural form: “Who will go for us?” to affirm that He is the one God, the Trinity, or the God of three Hypostases.

6.7.0.en: The Holy God, the Three Hypostases, accepted Isaiah's offer, and said to him: “Go” [9]. God did not want to send Isaiah to receive honor or glory, but to enter into bitterness with a people who reject the truth... For service is not Church positions or honors, but it is spiritual striving for the washing of the feet of others and urging them to accept the truth, and this through the holy altar that sanctifies the inner lips and gives the effective word of God in the life of the servant and those served.

6.7.1.en: The Lord put His words in the prophet's mouth: “Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not” [9]. The Lord put in Isaiah's mouth many prophecies about the Lord Christ and His saving work; and they were fulfilled at the coming of the Lord Christ: they heard and saw but did not believe in Him, because their inner insight had been struck with blindness; this is the opposite of the disciples to whom the Lord said: “Blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear” (Mt 13:11-16).

6.7.2.en: St. John Chrysostom says of this people: [They see how He casts out demons and they say: He has a devil; they see those raised from the dead and do not worship Him, but think of killing Him.]

6.7.3.en: We have already studied this prophecy in our explanation of the Gospel according to Matthew the Evangelist, chapter 13, so I will be content here with St. Augustine's comment on the question: Why are the Jews blamed for their unbelief, since God blinded their eyes?

6.7.4.en: [They were not able to believe because Isaiah prophesied this, and he prophesied because God had told him beforehand what their state would be. But if you ask: What is the cause of their inability to believe? I answer at once: They were unwilling. God saw their corrupt will, and therefore told the prophet beforehand, because the future is not hidden from Him... God blinded them and hardened them merely by leaving them and withdrawing His help from them.]

6.7.5.en: St. Irenaeus answers the same question, saying: [They are struck with blindness because of their unbelief in God, for they look toward Him and do not see Him, because to them He is as though He did not exist; just as the sun, His creature, afflicts those of weak sight so that they cannot see its light. But to those who believe in Him and follow Him, He gives a fuller and greater enlightenment to their minds.]

6.8.0.en: This is the interpretation of the prophet's words: “Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed” [10]. It is noted here that God does not ascribe the people to Himself, but calls them “this people,” and this usually happens when God declares His wrath against them and counts them unworthy to belong to Him because of the fatness of their hearts, the heaviness of their ears and the blindness of their eyes, that is, because of violence (hardness), disobedience and spiritual ignorance.

6.8.1.en: This prophecy points to the Jews' denial of the Lord Christ at His coming, as it also points to the denial of the words of prophecy in the days of Isaiah, so that they fall under captivity and ruin comes upon them at the hands of Sennacherib the Assyrian.

6.9.0.en: The prophet Isaiah grieved when he realized the weight of the responsibility laid upon him and the troubles and sufferings awaiting him, as he also grieved when he realized what would befall the people of destruction, so that the cities become waste without inhabitant and the houses without man and the land be desolate and waste [11], and he cried: “How long, O Lord GOD?” [11]. Was he asking: How long will this people remain in hardness?! Or was he asking: How long shall I proclaim prophecies so bitter and harsh?!

6.10.0.en: The Lord disclosed to him the state of the people after their breaking before Sennacherib, and declared that even if a tenth remains in the land [13], He will return and raise up the people through this remnant and make of them a holy seed. In this he prophesies concerning the captivity and what happens after the captivity. At the same time it is regarded as a prophecy concerning the captivity of the Jews in their denial of faith in the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world, but in the last days a remnant remains that returns to faith in Him. The Apostle Paul says: “That hardness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved” (Rom 11:25-26).
